item.research_question: How can morphology and surface chemistry be engineered to create inexpensive electrocatalysts that maintain high activity and stability for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) across a wide pH range at high current densities?
item.material_system: Flat platinum foil, molybdenum disulfide (MoS2) microspheres composed of radially aligned nanosheets, and MoS2 microspheres decorated with molybdenum carbide (Mo2C) nanoparticles (MoS2/Mo2C)
item.processing_route: Two-step synthesis: (1) Hydrothermal growth of MoS2 microspheres on Ti foil at 180 °C for 24 h; (2) Chemical vapor deposition (CVD) at 750 °C for 20–100 min using Ar/H2/CH4 (100/30/10 sccm) to convert MoS2 edges to Mo2C nanoparticles
item.test_conditions: Electrochemical testing in 1.0 M KOH (alkaline) and 0.5 M H2SO4 (acidic) electrolytes; current densities up to 1000 mA cm−2; 24 h stability tests; cyclic voltammetry (50 mV s−1) and linear sweep voltammetry (5 mV s−1)
key_findings: MoS2/Mo2C achieved overpotentials of 227 mV in acidic medium and 220 mV in alkaline medium at a high current density of 1000 mA cm−2
Tafel slopes for MoS2/Mo2C were 53 mV dec−1 in acidic medium and 44 mV dec−1 in alkaline medium
The ratio of overpotential to current density (Rη/j) for MoS2/Mo2C remained small (~45 mV dec−1) at high currents, whereas Pt foil increased to >120 mV dec−1
Contact angles for 1.0 M KOH were 82.3° (Pt), 53.8° (MoS2), and ~0° (MoS2/Mo2C), indicating superior wettability for the modified catalyst
Hydrogen bubbles on MoS2/Mo2C were smaller than 0.2 mm and released easily, whereas bubbles on Pt grew to >0.5 mm and adhered firmly
XPS analysis revealed that Mo2C surfaces were modified by –OH and –O groups formed during HER, which were absent on MoS2
DFT calculations showed a hydrogen free energy of ~0.1 eV and a water dissociation energy barrier of ~0.25 eV on oxygen-terminated Mo2C surfaces
MoS2/Mo2C showed negligible shift in polarization curves after 10,000 cycles and maintained performance after 24 h at 200 mA cm−2
item.mechanism: The authors propose that the MoS2/Mo2C catalyst's superior performance stems from two factors: (1) enhanced interfacial mass transfer due to micro/nano-scale roughness and surface oxygen groups that improve water affinity and bubble release, and (2) fast reaction kinetics where surface oxygen groups (–OH in acid, –O in alkali) formed on Mo2C during HER act as water dissociation promoters and facilitate hydrogen absorption/desorption
item.limitations: The text notes that while the catalyst works well at high current densities, many nonprecious catalysts and even Pt/C operate well only at low current densities (e.g., 10 mA cm−2) with large overpotentials at high densities; the study focuses on three specific model catalysts and does not test other pH conditions beyond acidic, neutral, and 6 M KOH
item.future_work: The authors suggest that the discovery of oxygen-terminated β-Mo2C for promoting water dissociation can be used to design other HER electrocatalysts that work well in both acidic and alkaline media, and that this strategy could be further developed to design even better electrocatalysts than MoS2/Mo2C
quotes: low overpotentials of 227 mV in acidic medium and 220 mV in alkaline medium at a high current density of 1000 mA cm−2
surface oxygen groups formed on molybdenum carbide during hydrogen evolution
oxygen-terminated β-Mo2C surface theoretically increases the interfacial mass transfer of the catalyst because oxygen terminates have a strong affinity to water and weak affinity to gas bubbles

records.text: Paper card. Question: How can morphology and surface chemistry be engineered to create inexpensive electrocatalysts that maintain high activity and stability for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) across a wide pH range at high current densities?. System: Flat platinum foil, molybdenum disulfide (MoS2) microspheres composed of radially aligned nanosheets, and MoS2 microspheres decorated with molybdenum carbide (Mo2C) nanoparticles (MoS2/Mo2C). Processing: Two-step synthesis: (1) Hydrothermal growth of MoS2 microspheres on Ti foil at 180 °C for 24 h; (2) Chemical vapor deposition (CVD) at 750 °C for 20–100 min using Ar/H2/CH4 (100/30/10 sccm) to convert MoS2 edges to Mo2C nanoparticles. Test conditions: Electrochemical testing in 1.0 M KOH (alkaline) and 0.5 M H2SO4 (acidic) electrolytes; current densities up to 1000 mA cm−2; 24 h stability tests; cyclic voltammetry (50 mV s−1) and linear sweep voltammetry (5 mV s−1). Findings: MoS2/Mo2C achieved overpotentials of 227 mV in acidic medium and 220 mV in alkaline medium at a high current density of 1000 mA cm−2; Tafel slopes for MoS2/Mo2C were 53 mV dec−1 in acidic medium and 44 mV dec−1 in alkaline medium; The ratio of overpotential to current density (Rη/j) for MoS2/Mo2C remained small (~45 mV dec−1) at high currents, whereas Pt foil increased to >120 mV dec−1; Contact angles for 1.0 M KOH were 82.3° (Pt), 53.8° (MoS2), and ~0° (MoS2/Mo2C), indicating superior wettability for the modified catalyst; Hydrogen bubbles on MoS2/Mo2C were smaller than 0.2 mm and released easily, whereas bubbles on Pt grew to >0.5 mm and adhered firmly; XPS analysis revealed that Mo2C surfaces were modified by –OH and –O groups formed during HER, which were absent on MoS2; DFT calculations showed a hydrogen free energy of ~0.1 eV and a water dissociation energy barrier of ~0.25 eV on oxygen-terminated Mo2C surfaces; MoS2/Mo2C showed negligible shift in polarization curves after 10,000 cycles and maintained performance after 24 h at 200 mA cm−2. Mechanism: The authors propose that the MoS2/Mo2C catalyst's superior performance stems from two factors: (1) enhanced interfacial mass transfer due to micro/nano-scale roughness and surface oxygen groups that improve water affinity and bubble release, and (2) fast reaction kinetics where surface oxygen groups (–OH in acid, –O in alkali) formed on Mo2C during HER act as water dissociation promoters and facilitate hydrogen absorption/desorption. Limitations: The text notes that while the catalyst works well at high current densities, many nonprecious catalysts and even Pt/C operate well only at low current densities (e.g., 10 mA cm−2) with large overpotentials at high densities; the study focuses on three specific model catalysts and does not test other pH conditions beyond acidic, neutral, and 6 M KOH. Future work: The authors suggest that the discovery of oxygen-terminated β-Mo2C for promoting water dissociation can be used to design other HER electrocatalysts that work well in both acidic and alkaline media, and that this strategy could be further developed to design even better electrocatalysts than MoS2/Mo2C. Quote: "low overpotentials of 227 mV in acidic medium and 220 mV in alkaline medium at a high current density of 1000 mA cm−2"
